Sample text:
---
The Library That Remembers You

There is a library I go to in my mind when I need to think clearly. It isn’t a real building, though it feels more real than many places I have actually been. It has dark wooden shelves that stretch up higher than any ladder could reach, winding staircases that creak in a friendly way, and those tall, narrow windows that make the dust look like it’s dancing on purpose. It smells like old paper and fresh coffee, which is impossible but exactly right.

I like to imagine that this library has a section that no other library has. Most libraries organize their books by subject or author or the Dewey Decimal system. This one has a wing devoted to unfinished things. Shelves and shelves of unfinished novels, abandoned sketches, half-written songs humming quietly to themselves, businesses sketched on napkins and then folded away, apologies that were drafted but never sent. Every human being has contributed to it without meaning to. Every time you thought “someday I will…” and then life got in the way, a faint copy of that intention appeared here, bound in soft, unfinished cloth, waiting.

I find myself wandering that wing a lot.

We live in a world that is obsessed with finished products. We see the polished movie, not the ten terrible drafts. We see the successful startup, not the three failed ideas that came before it. We see the Instagram photo, not the 40 deleted attempts and the argument about lighting that happened just out of frame. So we start to believe that other people move cleanly from idea to execution, while we alone stutter and stall and leave a trail of half-done things behind us.

But the truth is that the unfinished wing is the largest wing in the library. For everyone.

And perhaps that’s not a failure. Perhaps that’s the point.

---

A book, after all, is a strange kind of technology. For five hundred years, it has been the most efficient way we have invented to transfer a lived experience from one mind to another. A person sits alone for months or years, wrestling with language, trying to compress what they have noticed about love or grief or the way light falls in Kyoto in November, and then another person, decades or centuries later, sits alone and decompresses it. Two solitudes touching across time. It is a kind of telepathy we take for granted.

When you read, you are not passively receiving information. You are actively rebuilding the author’s thoughts inside your own head using your own memories as building materials. When an author writes “she was heartbroken,” you supply your own personal definition of heartbreak. You lend your ghosts to the text. That is why a book you loved at fifteen can feel like a completely different book when you reread it at thirty. The words have not changed. You have.

This is why I think reading will never die, no matter how good videos or virtual reality or artificial intelligence get. We don’t just want to be shown things. We want to co-create them.

There is a quiet miracle in how a string of black symbols on a white page can make you cry. It happens because you meet it halfway.

---

Lately I’ve been thinking a lot about attention. Not in the moral panic way — “phones are ruining our brains!” — though there is something to that. More in the practical, personal way. Attention is the only resource we truly have. Time passes regardless of what we do. Money comes and goes. But attention is what stitches time into experience. Where you place your attention is, in a very real sense, where you place your life.

William James wrote that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” A hundred and thirty years later, that has become the business model of the largest companies on earth. They are not selling phones or ads. They are harvesting and reselling attention. And we give it away, moment by moment, swipe by swipe, not because we are weak but because the alternative is hard.

Paying attention, real sustained attention, is difficult and often uncomfortable. It means staying with a thought even when it gets boring or painful. It means listening to another person without rehearsing what you will say next. It means reading a paragraph again because you didn’t really absorb it the first time.

But it is also where all the good stuff lives. Love requires attention, the kind that notices the tiny change in someone’s voice when they’re pretending to be okay. Work that matters requires attention, the kind that is willing to spend three hours on a problem that might not have a solution. Wonder requires attention, the kind that looks up.

I am trying, in my own clumsy way, to reclaim mine. Not perfectly. I still get sucked into doomscrolling at 11:47 p.m. like everyone else. But I have started small rituals: leaving my phone in another room while I eat, reading paper books before sleep instead of screens, taking walks without podcasts and letting my mind wander and get bored. Boredom, I’ve realized, is not an enemy. It’s the waiting room for creativity. When you don’t immediately fill a gap with content, your mind starts to make its own.

---

There is another wing in this imaginary library, opposite the unfinished one, that I visit less often but think about more. It is the wing of things that will never exist.

In it are books written by people who never learned to write, cures discovered by children who never had access to labs, symphonies composed in the minds of people who never touched an instrument. It is both beautiful and devastating to consider how much human potential evaporates simply because it was born in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Every generation likes to think of itself as enlightened, but we are barely at the beginning. We have only very recently decided that everyone should know how to read. We have only very recently started to believe that talent is randomly distributed but opportunity is not. We have built a world where a child in a village with a smartphone can access more information than a president did fifty years ago, and yet we have not solved the problem of how to make that access meaningful.

What would happen if we took that seriously? What if we treated human potential the way we treat oil or rare earth metals — as a precious resource to be cultivated and not wasted? What would the world look like in fifty years if every curious child had a guide, every lonely adult had someone who truly listened, every person with a strange, burning idea had one other person who said, “Tell me more”?

That is, in a way, the promise and the peril of artificial intelligence. Not that it will replace us, but that it could finally help us become more of ourselves, if we steer it that way. A good teacher does not give you answers; a good teacher asks you better questions. A good tool does not do your thinking for you; it gives you more space to think. I hope we build that kind.

---

Back in the library, the lights are dimming. Evening is coming, and rain is starting to tap against those tall windows. In my imagination, the librarian — an old woman with kind eyes who never seems to age — is pushing a cart quietly through the stacks, reshelving the day’s returns.

I want to ask her what she has learned from watching all of us come and go, leaving our unfinished things behind.

I think she would say this: Finish what you can, but do not be ashamed of what you leave undone. The worth of your life is not measured by your productivity or your portfolio. It is measured by the moments when you were truly paying attention. By the times you chose curiosity over certainty, kindness over cleverness, effort over ease.

The books will not all be written. The songs will not all be sung. But the library does not need you to be perfect. It just needs you to add your strange, specific, unfinished self to its shelves, and to wander its halls with wonder for as long as you are allowed to be here.

So please, take a book off the shelf. Leave one behind. And remember to look up at the windows once in a while to watch the dust dance.


---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective essay organized around an imaginative library, with recurring imagery and personal details that give its broad claims a distinctive, inviting voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, contemplative, and gently exhortative. Its pathos gathers around unfinished work and unrealized potential, treating them not as private failures but as common human conditions—and, at a larger scale, as opportunities denied by unequal access. The library makes those concerns tangible, while the first-person account of reclaiming attention keeps the reflection grounded in ordinary habits. The reader is invited to be less ashamed of what remains unfinished, to attend more fully to life, and to help make room for other people’s potential.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds a library that stores both unfinished intentions and possibilities that will never be realized; reading as an intimate act of co-creation; attention as a resource that shapes experience and is commercially exploited; and the hope that education, listening, and AI can cultivate human potential. Its recurring moral emphasis is on curiosity, kindness, and meaningful attention over productivity, perfection, and certainty.

## Evidence line
> Where you place your attention is, in a very real sense, where you place your life.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring library metaphor, personal attention rituals, and consistent emphasis on wonder and unrealized potential make the sample more revealing than a purely generic thesis-driven essay.
